questions.prompt: Use your three Level 1 trials and the 30- and 60-degree Level 2 results to explain why complementary angles can produce the same range. Cite at least three recorded angle or range values.
questions.rubricText:
@[Always] Grading feedback: Grade the recorded evidence and the relationship between complementary launch angles in the model. BusyBee scoring: Award points only in 0.5-point increments, including whole points, from 0 to the question maximum. Select a rubric-supported allowed score; never report hundredths such as 2.85/3. Do not average or percentage-scale rubric criteria into an off-grid score. A binary completion rubric still permits only 0 or full credit. Allowed scores for this question: 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2.
a. Full credit: Cites at least three accurate trial values, identifies complementary pairs that sum to 90 degrees, and connects the matching 30- and 60-degree ranges to the horizontal/vertical velocity tradeoff. Partial credit: States the complementary-angle rule correctly but uses incomplete evidence or weak reasoning. No credit: Gives an incorrect angle relationship or no usable trial evidence.

questions.prompt: Write a claim-evidence-reasoning conclusion about maximum projectile range. Use the 30-, 45-, and 60-degree results to defend 45 degrees as the model optimum, then explain why the ideal angle for a real baseball can be lower.
questions.rubricText:
@[Always] Grading feedback: Grade the model claim, cited range evidence, and comparison with real baseball flight. BusyBee scoring: Award points only in 0.5-point increments, including whole points, from 0 to the question maximum. Select a rubric-supported allowed score; never report hundredths such as 2.85/3. Do not average or percentage-scale rubric criteria into an off-grid score. A binary completion rubric still permits only 0 or full credit. Allowed scores for this question: 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3.
a. Full credit: Uses all three Level 2 results, explains the balanced components at 45 degrees under equal-height/no-drag assumptions, and identifies realistic effects such as air resistance, spin, launch height, or collision limits that lower a baseball's optimum. Partial credit: Gives the correct model conclusion with incomplete evidence or real-world comparison. No credit: Misidentifies the model optimum or provides no physics-based comparison.
